query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a modest concentration (for example, ~5 atomic%) of aluminum to a refractory high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of a stable and adherent alumina scale at high temperatures in an oxidizing environment, reducing oxygen ingress and lowering the oxidation rate by at least 20% compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., Mo-Nb-Ta-W-V) in the as-cast condition.
generation.intervention: Incorporate approximately 5 atomic% aluminum into the alloy composition through a suitable process, such as mechanical alloying or co-melting, to increase the probability of forming a protective alumina layer.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (∼1200°C) in air for at least 24 hours of continuous heating.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniform distribution of aluminum within the microstructure to facilitate the formation of a continuous, protective aluminum oxide surface scale.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures in an oxygen-containing environment, the added aluminum preferentially oxidizes to form a dense Al2O3 barrier, limiting oxygen diffusion into the alloy and reducing further oxidation damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under these conditions, the Al-doped alloy will exhibit a measurable reduction (≥20%) in mass gain and oxide scale thickness compared to the undoped alloy over the same exposure time.
generation.baseline: The performance (oxidation rate and scale thickness) of the undoped refractory high-entropy alloy under identical test conditions, which typically experiences higher mass gain and deeper oxygen ingress.
generation.boundary: Major benefits are expected above ~1000–1200°C in strongly oxidizing environments; insufficient aluminum content or lower temperatures may prevent formation of a stable alumina layer, reducing the protective effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact aluminum content and processing conditions needed to form a continuous alumina layer without compromising mechanical properties require further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: (1) baseline composition without Al and (2) identical composition but with ~5 at% Al added. Expose both sets to 1200°C in static air for 24 hours, followed by cooling to room temperature. Characterize oxidation via weight change measurements, cross-sectional microscopy, and X-ray diffraction of the oxide scales.
measurements: Mass change before and after exposure (to assess oxidation kinetics)
Cross-sectional oxide scale thickness using metallographic analysis
Composition and structure of the oxide layer via X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not show at least a 20% reduction in total mass gain or a visibly thinner, more uniform alumina scale compared to the undoped alloy under these conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.
